title: Understanding Colour Theory
section: 12. Web Design School - Create a Website that People Love
summary: Colour choice should be deliberate: each dominant colour carries a mood, and colours are combined using relationships on the colour wheel. Covers analogous, complementary, triadic and square schemes, plus tools (Adobe Color, Color Hunt) for getting hex codes.

concepts.heading: Colour sets the mood
points: The predominant colour of a design communicates a message before any text is read. A palette that contradicts the brand (for example earthy brown on something cheerful) feels off, while a palette matching the message feels intentional.
Red: love, energy, intensity. Common in advertising for cars and anything meant to feel powerful.
Yellow: joy, intellect, attention. It is extremely attention-grabbing, so it suits logos and headlines but tires the eyes in long reading areas; avoid a full yellow background behind article text.
Green: freshness, growth, safety. A safe default for food and grocery brands.
Blue: stability, trust, serenity. Popular with finance and payments companies; a study she mentions found people wearing blue were trusted more by interviewers.
Purple: royalty, wealth, femininity. Sometimes used by lenders targeting women.
Pick colours by asking what message the user should receive, not by personal favourites.

concepts.heading: Combining colours with the colour wheel
points: Real designs normally use two or three colours, so the relationships between them matter. This is the most systematic part of colour theory.
Analogous palette: colours adjacent on the wheel. Very harmonious; works for navigation bars, page bodies, and a logo against its background. Weakness: little contrast, so nothing stands out.
Complementary (clashing) palette: colours from opposite sides of the wheel. Creates strong pop and makes each colour look more vivid (example: red meat displayed against green plastic foliage).
Do not use complementary colours for text on a background. The vibration is hard to read. Reserve them for logos, icons, accents and elements that should stand apart.
Triadic palette: three colours forming an equilateral triangle on the wheel. Square palette: four colours forming a square.
(Extra) Common practical rule: one dominant colour, one secondary, and one accent (roughly 60/30/10 usage).

concepts.heading: Tools
points: Adobe Color: pick a harmony rule (analogous, complementary, triadic, square) and drag on the wheel until the palette matches the project's mood, then copy the hex codes into your CSS.
colorhunt.co: curated palettes by designers; browse the popular or trending sections and copy hex codes directly.
A consistent, brand-appropriate palette makes a site look cohesive and can be playful without feeling chaotic.

code_examples.caption: (Extra) Putting a palette into CSS as custom properties

pitfalls: Choosing colours because they are favourites rather than because they suit the message.
Using complementary colours for text and its background.
Large yellow backgrounds behind body copy.
Using too many unrelated hues instead of a small scheme.

Tasks: 1) define a palette as CSS variables; 2) build an analogous version of a navbar; 3) add a complementary accent button; 4) fix a page that uses complementary text/background; 5) swap hex codes from Color Hunt.
Starter code idea: a landing page whose colours are all hard-coded and clashing.
